claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten-based plasma-facing components is governed by dislocation climb.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten-based plasma-facing components is governed by dislocation climb.
Vacancy diffusion facilitates dislocation climb in tungsten.
Ta alloying can modify the vacancy-mediated deformation behavior of tungsten.
The proposed initial material is ultra-high-purity tungsten with intrinsic vacancy formation energies and diffusion kinetics.
Adding Ta to tungsten alters vacancy formation energies.
Adding Ta to tungsten alters vacancy migration rates.
The controlled comparison is between Ta-alloyed tungsten and undoped tungsten tested under identical conditions.
Mechanical testing is proposed at 1200–1500 °C under controlled strain rate in vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
Vacuum or inert test environments minimize oxidation and other extraneous reactions.
TEM and related analyses can characterize the relevant dislocation structures and vacancy-related microstructural features.
Ta-induced changes in vacancy kinetics accelerate dislocation climb.
Ta-induced changes in vacancy kinetics promote dynamic recovery.
A reduced barrier for dislocation climb lowers high-temperature yield stress.
A reduced barrier for dislocation climb improves high-temperature ductility and toughness.
W–Ta alloys are predicted to have lower yield stress than undoped tungsten under the specified high-temperature conditions.
W–Ta alloys are predicted to exhibit greater plastic strain and toughness than undoped tungsten.
W–Ta alloys are predicted to exhibit more dislocation climb and dynamic recovery than undoped tungsten.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to tungsten-based alloys up to approximately 1500 °C when oxidation and other extraneous effects are minimized.
Failure to observe statistically significant mechanical improvements or enhanced climb and vacancy-related features in W–Ta relative to pure W would falsify the hypothesis.
